Find Your Local Beekeeping Club or Association

Find Your Local Beekeeping Club or Association

Connecting with experienced beekeepers is the fastest way to succeed with your hives. This directory lists active beekeeping clubs, state associations, and national organizations across the United States. Whether you're looking for hands-on mentorship, monthly meetings, or swarm call lists, your local club is an invaluable resource.

Why Every Beekeeper Should Join a Local Club

The difference between struggling beekeepers and thriving ones often comes down to one thing: community. A good local club gives you access to experienced mentors who've already made the mistakes you're about to make—and they'll help you avoid them.

Here's what you actually get from membership:

  • Mentorship that saves money: A mentor can diagnose a failing hive in 10 minutes. Learning it from a book takes months. That one piece of advice—catching a disease early, fixing a laying worker problem, or timing a split correctly—often pays for years of dues.
  • Group equipment purchases: Clubs negotiate bulk discounts on hive boxes, frames, and extractors. You'll save 15-25% compared to retail prices, and you'll have vetted recommendations on what actually works.
  • Swarm retrieval networks: Your club's swarm call list means free bees when someone in your area spots a swarm. That's $100-200 in free package bees, just from being connected.
  • Shared equipment: Most clubs maintain libraries of extractors, uncapping knives, and other expensive gear. Borrow instead of buy.
  • Hands-on hive inspections: Watching an experienced beekeeper work a hive teaches you more than any video. You see the rhythm, learn to read the brood pattern, and get comfortable with bees.
  • Local knowledge: Your club knows which plants bloom when in your area, which pests are problems this year, and which treatment protocols work best in your climate. Generic beekeeping advice doesn't account for your specific region.

Beginners especially benefit. You're not going to feel stupid asking questions—everyone in that room asked the same questions when they started. The club exists partly to help people like you succeed.

National Beekeeping Organizations

These organizations provide resources, advocacy, and community at the national level. Many offer insurance programs, legislative support, and publications that complement your local club membership.

American Beekeeping Federation (ABF)

The largest national organization representing beekeepers of all sizes. ABF advocates for beekeeper interests in Washington, publishes the American Bee Journal, and organizes the annual convention. Membership includes access to their insurance program and legislative updates. Strong focus on commercial and sideline beekeepers, but welcomes hobbyists.

Website: abfnet.org

Apiary Inspectors of America (AIA)

Professional organization for state apiary inspectors and beekeeping regulators. While primarily for inspectors, beekeepers benefit from their work on disease management standards and hive inspection protocols. They publish guidelines that inform best practices across the country.

Website: apiaryinspectors.org

American Honey Producers Association (AHPA)

Focused on commercial honey production and advocacy. If you're running bees for income or considering it, AHPA provides market data, legislative representation, and networking with other producers.

Website: americanhoneyproducers.org

Bee Culture Magazine / American Bee Journal

While not membership organizations, these publications are essential reading. Bee Culture focuses on practical management; American Bee Journal covers research and commercial operations. Most clubs have back issues available.

Project Apis m. (PAm)

Nonprofit focused on bee health research and funding. They don't offer membership in the traditional sense, but they fund research that directly impacts how we manage hives. Worth following for their research summaries.

Website: projectapism.org

The Bee Informed Partnership

University-based research network tracking colony losses and hive health across North America. Free annual survey participation helps beekeepers benchmark their operation and contributes to national data on what works.

Website: beeinformed.org
